subject: math
domain: Conditional Probability and the Rules of Probability
cluster: Understand independence and conditional probability and use them to interpret data
intro: These problems build, complete, and read two-way frequency tables, then use them to compute marginal, joint, and conditional probabilities and to test whether two events are independent. Write every probability as an exact reduced fraction unless a decimal is asked for.

items.prompt:
A survey of $50$ people records whether each owns a dog and whether each owns a cat. The two-way table below is complete. Find the grand total and verify it equals the sum of the row totals.

$$\begin{array}{c|cc|c} & \text{Cat} & \text{No cat} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Dog} & 8 & 14 & 22 \\ \text{No dog} & 6 & 22 & 28 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 14 & 36 & 50 \end{array}$$

What is the grand total of people surveyed?

steps: Add the two row totals: $22 + 28 = 50$.
Check against the column totals: $14 + 36 = 50$. They agree.
The grand total is $50$ people.

items.prompt: Using the table from problem $1$ (grand total $50$, of whom $22$ own a dog), find $P(\text{owns a dog})$. Write the probability as a reduced fraction.

steps: A marginal probability is a row total over the grand total: $P(\text{owns a dog}) = \dfrac{22}{50}$.
Reduce by dividing numerator and denominator by $2$: $\dfrac{22}{50} = \dfrac{11}{25}$.
So $P(\text{owns a dog}) = \dfrac{11}{25}$.

items.prompt: A two-way table of $40$ students classifies each by grade level (senior or junior) and whether they play a sport. The cell for students who are seniors and play a sport holds $15$. Find $P(\text{senior and plays a sport})$ as a reduced fraction.

steps: A joint probability is one cell count over the grand total: $P(\text{senior and plays a sport}) = \dfrac{15}{40}$.
Reduce by dividing numerator and denominator by $5$: $\dfrac{15}{40} = \dfrac{3}{8}$.
So $P(\text{senior and plays a sport}) = \dfrac{3}{8}$.

items.prompt:
The two-way table below is missing one row total. Find the missing value labeled $x$.

$$\begin{array}{c|cc|c} & \text{Yes} & \text{No} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Group A} & 12 & 8 & x \\ \text{Group B} & 5 & 15 & 20 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 17 & 23 & 40 \end{array}$$

steps: A row total is the sum of the cells across that row: $x = 12 + 8 = 20$.
Check the grand total: $20 + 20 = 40$, which matches the column totals $17 + 23 = 40$.

items.prompt: From a complete two-way table with grand total $100$, exactly $24$ people answered 'Yes' to a question. Find $P(\text{Yes})$ and write it as a decimal.

steps: A marginal probability is the column total over the grand total: $P(\text{Yes}) = \dfrac{24}{100}$.
Convert to a decimal: $\dfrac{24}{100} = 0.24$.
So $P(\text{Yes}) = 0.24$.

items.prompt: Of $40$ students, $22$ are seniors and the rest are juniors. Among the seniors, $15$ play a sport; among the juniors, $9$ play a sport. Construct the two-way table (class versus plays a sport) and report all four interior cell counts, the row totals, the column totals, and the grand total.
items.answer: Seniors: $15$ sport, $7$ no sport (row total $22$). Juniors: $9$ sport, $9$ no sport (row total $18$). Columns: $24$ sport, $16$ no sport. Grand total $40$.

steps: There are $40 - 22 = 18$ juniors.
Seniors who do not play a sport: $22 - 15 = 7$. Juniors who do not play a sport: $18 - 9 = 9$.
Column totals: sport $= 15 + 9 = 24$; no sport $= 7 + 9 = 16$.
Check: row totals $22 + 18 = 40$ and column totals $24 + 16 = 40$, so the grand total is $40$.

The completed table is $\begin{array}{c|cc|c} & \text{Sport} & \text{No sport} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Senior} & 15 & 7 & 22 \\ \text{Junior} & 9 & 9 & 18 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 24 & 16 & 40 \end{array}$

items.prompt: Using the table from problem $6$ ($15$ of the $22$ seniors play a sport), find the conditional probability $P(\text{plays a sport} \mid \text{senior})$. Write it as a fraction.

steps: Conditioning on 'senior' restricts the sample space to the $22$ seniors, so the denominator is the senior row total.
Of those $22$ seniors, $15$ play a sport: $P(\text{plays a sport} \mid \text{senior}) = \dfrac{15}{22}$.
$\dfrac{15}{22}$ is already in lowest terms since $\gcd(15,22)=1$.
So $P(\text{plays a sport} \mid \text{senior}) = \dfrac{15}{22}$.

items.prompt: Using the same table from problem $6$ (the 'sport' column total is $24$, of whom $15$ are seniors), find $P(\text{senior} \mid \text{plays a sport})$. Write it as a reduced fraction.

steps: Conditioning on 'plays a sport' restricts the sample space to the $24$ sport players, so the denominator is the sport column total.
Of those $24$ sport players, $15$ are seniors: $P(\text{senior} \mid \text{plays a sport}) = \dfrac{15}{24}$.
Reduce by dividing by $3$: $\dfrac{15}{24} = \dfrac{5}{8}$.
Note this differs from $P(\text{plays a sport} \mid \text{senior}) = \dfrac{15}{22}$ because the conditioning total changed.

items.prompt: Using the table from problem $6$, compute $P(\text{plays a sport} \mid \text{senior})$ and $P(\text{plays a sport} \mid \text{junior})$, then state which class is more likely to play a sport.
items.answer: $P(\text{sport}\mid\text{senior}) = \frac{15}{22} \approx 0.682$ and $P(\text{sport}\mid\text{junior}) = \frac{1}{2}$; seniors are more likely to play a sport.

steps: Seniors: $15$ of $22$ play a sport, so $P(\text{sport} \mid \text{senior}) = \dfrac{15}{22} \approx 0.682$.
Juniors: $9$ of $18$ play a sport, so $P(\text{sport} \mid \text{junior}) = \dfrac{9}{18} = \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.5$.
Seniors are more likely to play a sport than juniors.

items.prompt:
A clinic tests $80$ patients. The two-way table below records test result (positive or negative) versus whether the patient has the condition. Find $P(\text{has the condition} \mid \text{tested positive})$ as a reduced fraction.

$$\begin{array}{c|cc|c} & \text{Positive} & \text{Negative} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Condition} & 18 & 2 & 20 \\ \text{No condition} & 12 & 48 & 60 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 30 & 50 & 80 \end{array}$$

steps: Conditioning on 'tested positive' restricts to the $30$ patients in the Positive column.
Of those $30$, the ones who actually have the condition number $18$: $P(\text{condition} \mid \text{positive}) = \dfrac{18}{30}$.
Reduce by dividing by $6$: $\dfrac{18}{30} = \dfrac{3}{5}$.
So $P(\text{has the condition} \mid \text{tested positive}) = \dfrac{3}{5}$.

items.prompt: Using the table from problem $6$ (grand total $40$: $P(\text{senior}) = \frac{22}{40}$, $P(\text{sport}) = \frac{24}{40}$, $P(\text{senior and sport}) = \frac{15}{40}$), test whether the events 'is a senior' and 'plays a sport' are independent using the product rule. State your conclusion.
items.answer: Not independent: $P(A)\cdot P(B) = \frac{33}{100} = 0.33$ but $P(A \cap B) = \frac{15}{40} = 0.375$, and $0.33 \ne 0.375$.

steps: Let $A = \text{senior}$ and $B = \text{plays a sport}$. The events are independent only if $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\cdot P(B)$.
Compute the product: $P(A)\cdot P(B) = \dfrac{22}{40}\cdot\dfrac{24}{40} = \dfrac{528}{1600} = \dfrac{33}{100} = 0.33$.
Compute the joint probability directly from the cell: $P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{15}{40} = 0.375$.
Since $0.33 \ne 0.375$, the equality fails.
The events are not independent: being a senior is associated with a higher chance of playing a sport.

items.prompt:
In a sample of $200$ commuters, the table below records mode of travel (drives or takes transit) versus arrival (on time or late). Decide whether 'drives' and 'on time' are independent by comparing $P(\text{on time} \mid \text{drives})$ with $P(\text{on time})$. State your conclusion.

$$\begin{array}{c|cc|c} & \text{On time} & \text{Late} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Drives} & 90 & 30 & 120 \\ \text{Transit} & 60 & 20 & 80 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 150 & 50 & 200 \end{array}$$

steps: Conditional: of the $120$ drivers, $90$ are on time, so $P(\text{on time} \mid \text{drives}) = \dfrac{90}{120} = \dfrac{3}{4}$.
Marginal: of all $200$ commuters, $150$ are on time, so $P(\text{on time}) = \dfrac{150}{200} = \dfrac{3}{4}$.
The two values are equal: $\dfrac{3}{4} = \dfrac{3}{4}$.
Since $P(\text{on time} \mid \text{drives}) = P(\text{on time})$, knowing a commuter drives does not change the probability of being on time.
Therefore the events 'drives' and 'on time' are independent.

items.prompt:
A study of $120$ households classifies each by whether it has children (yes or no) and whether it subscribes to a streaming service (yes or no). The table below is missing the count $n$ of households with children that subscribe. Find the value of $n$ that makes 'has children' and 'subscribes' independent.

$$\begin{array}{c|cc|c} & \text{Subscribes} & \text{No} & \text{Total} \\ \hline \text{Children} & n & \; & 40 \\ \text{No children} & \; & \; & 80 \\ \hline \text{Total} & 60 & 60 & 120 \end{array}$$

steps: Let $A = \text{has children}$ and $B = \text{subscribes}$. Independence requires $P(A \cap B) = P(A)\cdot P(B)$.
From the margins, $P(A) = \dfrac{40}{120} = \dfrac{1}{3}$ and $P(B) = \dfrac{60}{120} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
So $P(A \cap B) = \dfrac{1}{3}\cdot\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{6}$.
The cell count is $n = P(A \cap B)\cdot(\text{grand total}) = \dfrac{1}{6}\cdot 120 = 20$.
So $n = 20$ makes the two events independent.

items.prompt: Using the completed table from problem $13$ with $n = 20$, verify independence a second way by checking that $P(\text{subscribes} \mid \text{has children})$ equals $P(\text{subscribes})$. Show both probabilities.
items.answer: Both equal $\frac{1}{2}$: $P(\text{subscribes} \mid \text{has children}) = \frac{20}{40} = \frac{1}{2}$ and $P(\text{subscribes}) = \frac{60}{120} = \frac{1}{2}$, confirming independence.

steps: With $n = 20$, the 'children' row has $20$ subscribers out of a row total of $40$.
Conditional: $P(\text{subscribes} \mid \text{has children}) = \dfrac{20}{40} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
Marginal: $P(\text{subscribes}) = \dfrac{60}{120} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
Since $\dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{1}{2}$, the conditional equals the marginal.
This confirms the events are independent, matching the product-rule result from problem $13$.

items.prompt: A school surveys $60$ students about whether they walk to school and whether they eat breakfast. Of the students, $36$ walk and $24$ do not; $40$ eat breakfast and $20$ do not. Among the walkers, $28$ eat breakfast. Test whether 'walks to school' and 'eats breakfast' are independent, and interpret the result in context.
items.answer: Not independent: $P(\text{breakfast} \mid \text{walks}) = \frac{28}{36} = \frac{7}{9} \approx 0.778$ but $P(\text{breakfast}) = \frac{40}{60} = \frac{2}{3} \approx 0.667$. Since they differ, knowing a student walks raises the chance they eat breakfast, so the events are dependent.

steps: Let $A = \text{walks to school}$ and $B = \text{eats breakfast}$.
Conditional: of the $36$ walkers, $28$ eat breakfast, so $P(B \mid A) = \dfrac{28}{36} = \dfrac{7}{9} \approx 0.778$.
Marginal: of all $60$ students, $40$ eat breakfast, so $P(B) = \dfrac{40}{60} = \dfrac{2}{3} \approx 0.667$.
Compare: $\dfrac{7}{9} \ne \dfrac{2}{3}$ (equivalently $0.778 \ne 0.667$), so the equality $P(B \mid A) = P(B)$ fails.
The events are not independent. In context, students who walk to school are more likely to eat breakfast than students overall, so walking and eating breakfast are associated.
